messages.subject: multiple coefficients for a covariate
parts:
I would like to run a logistic regression  model in which I have multiple covariates, each being multiplied by a common coefficient (having a normal prior) and a covariate specific coefficient with a bernoulli prior (therefore taking values 0 or 1).
The model is set up this way in order to determine the importance of each  the variables, the higher the posterior mean of the covariate specific coefficient, the higher the importance of the variable.
Is there any way to fit this type of model in INLA?
 
Furthermore, I would like to add another complexity to the model. Each variable is measured with error and there is a variable in the dataset containing the standard errors. I would like to implement a Berkson measurement error model by specifying that the true values are normally distributed with mean the observed values and precision given by 1/ variance.
 
I looked mostly at the references for the INLA package and I could not find anything similar to the model that I would like to implement. I was wandering if the INLA R package is less flexible that the INLA program itself
and if more complex models requires the use of the INLA program (without the R interface).
 
I would greatly appreciate if somebody could give me some directions on how to implement these models in INLA or where to find some references/ examples for similar models.
Thank you in advance for your answer,
Georgiana

On Sat, 2012-03-17 at 11:19 -0700, newuser wrote:
> I would like to run a logistic regression model in which I
> have multiple covariates, each being multiplied by a common
> coefficient (having a normal prior) and a covariate specific
> coefficient with a bernoulli prior (therefore taking values 0 or 1).
> The model is set up this way in order to determine the importance of
> each the variables, the higher the posterior mean of the covariate
> specific coefficient, the higher the importance of the variable.
> Is there any way to fit this type of model in INLA?

you cannot have binary variables in a model in INLA. you can run
multiple instances if INLA for each configuration of your binary
variables, and compute/estimate the marginal likelihood. then you can,
for all the binary configurations you have, simply sum out and compute
the marginal for each one, using the marginal likelihood from INLA and
your own prior. that is pretty cool... well, I am implicity assuming
that you do not have toooo many of these binary variables.

I didn't understand really your other question, please post a more
detailed description or the math which is easier.

> Furthermore, I would like to add another complexity to the model. Each
> variable is measured with error and there is a variable in the
> dataset containing the standard errors. I would like to implement a
> Berkson measurement error model by specifying that the true values are
> normally distributed with mean the observed values and precision given
> by 1/ variance.

Contact Andrea Riebler in Zurich about this, she is working on such
models.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] multiple coefficients for a covariate
parts:
On Mon, 2012-03-19 at 09:35 -0700, newuser wrote:
> I have attached a file describing the model. There are nine continuous
> covariates (x1,x2,...x9) each having a common coefficient (beta_1)
> with a normal prior and a covariate specific coefficient (w1,w2,...w9)
> having a Bernoulli prior. The covariates are measured with error and
> there is a variable in the dataset containing the standard deviations
> (which I would like to specify as prior standard deviation). I would
> also like to add some additional covariates (some binary and some
> continuous)
> Based on the previous answer, does it mean that the model cannot be
> fitted directly in INLA because the covariate specific coefficients
> (w_1,...w_9) are binary and because I will have to add binary
> covariates? Are there any examples on how to run multiple instances
> of INLA and compute the marginal likelihood for binary variables? Is
> my model too complex to do this approach?

so this means you have 2^9 = 512 different models, not a huge number. a
common 'beta' only means that we can add the covariates up, for all
those i's where w_i=1. attached is a simplistic example, showing what
is going on. the key observation, is that conditional on the {w_i}'s,
you have a LGM.

In your case you'll want a 9-dimensional loop or better, list of all
the 512 combinations of {w_i}'s, and to do the summing out in the same
way, to get the marginal probability for covariate_i being part of the
model. (or any joint probabilites can also be compuated, of'course.)
